title: De Spectaculis
author: Tertullian

passages.original: post hunc Numa Pompilius Marti et Robigini fecit (nam et robiginis deam finxerunt); dehinc Tullus Hostibus, dehinc Ancus Martius et ceteri. Qui quos quem per ordinem et quibus idolis ludos instituerint, positum est apud Suetonium Tranquillum vel a quibus Tranquillus accepit. Sed haec satis erunt ad originis de idololatria reatum.
passages.english: After him Numa Pompilius held [games] for Mars and Robigo (for they even invented a goddess of blight); next Tullus Hostilius, next Ancus Martius, and the rest. Who instituted games, which ones, in what order, and for which idols, is set out in Suetonius Tranquillus, or in those from whom Tranquillus took it. But this will be enough to establish the guilt of their origin in idolatry.
passages.notes: "Hostibus" is evidently a corruption of "Hostilius" (Tullus Hostilius) and is translated as such. "Robigini" is taken as the deity Robigo/Robigus, the god of crop blight (robigo, rust or mildew). "Qui quos quem" is garbled in the text; it is rendered by the sense, as who instituted which games.

passages.original: Res equestris retro simplex: de dorso agebatur, et utique communis usus reus non erat. Sed cum ad ludos coactus est, transiit a dei munere ad daemoniorum officia. Itaque Castori et Polluci deputatur haec species, quibus equos a Mercurio distributos Stesichorus docet. Sed et Neptunus equestris est, quem Graeci i(/ppion appellant. Seiugas vero Iovi, quadrigas Soli, bigas Lunae sanxerunt. Sed et primus Erichthonius currus et quattuor ausus iungere equos rapidusque rotis insistere victor.
passages.english: Horsemanship was formerly a simple matter: it was done from the horse's back, and certainly its common use was not guilty [of anything]. But when it was forced into the games, it passed from being a gift of God to the service of demons. Accordingly this kind [of spectacle] is assigned to Castor and Pollux, to whom, as Stesichorus teaches, horses were allotted by Mercury. But Neptune too is equestrian, whom the Greeks call *Hippios* ["of horses"]. And they consecrated the six-horse team to Jupiter, the four-horse team to the Sun, the two-horse team to the Moon. But also "Erichthonius first dared to yoke chariots and four horses, and to stand victorious on the swift wheels."
passages.notes: "i(/ppion" is a Beta-code rendering of Greek ἵππιον (Hippios, "of horses"). The final sentence is a quotation of Virgil, Georgics 3.113–114, with slight adaptation. "Seiugas" = seiuges, six-horse chariots.
